findings.text: A per-process timer slack control is exposed as a readable and writable file. Writing supplies a decimal slack value for the process owning the file, while reading reports the current value. Opening the file attaches the owning inode so later operations can resolve the target process.

A process may always adjust its own slack, but changing or viewing another process demands scheduling privilege in that process user namespace plus a security module approval. Real-time and deadline scheduled processes always end up with zero slack, and a written zero for other processes restores the inherited default rather than disabling slack.

Credential checks for foreign targets run under read-side critical section protection, and the slack value itself is read and updated only while holding the target task lock. The task reference obtained from the file inode is released on every path.
The timer slack file uses the sequential file helpers for reading, seeking and release, with a custom open routine and a custom write routine around a single-shot display callback.

Per-process directories share generic helpers that create inodes from table entries, resolve names by table scan, and enumerate entries for directory reads. Instantiation applies the entry mode and any custom operations, records the entry payload in the private inode, refreshes attributes from the live task, and splices the result into the dentry cache.

Name resolution walks the directory table linearly and compares both length and content, reporting missing when nothing matches or the owning task has exited. Directory enumeration always starts with the two dot entries and then maps the stored read position onto the table.

Security module attributes appear as small files whose content is provided by the security layer keyed on the file name and the stored module identifier. Reads fetch a freshly generated buffer and copy the requested span to user space before freeing it.

Attribute writes are tightly scoped: only the process that opened the file may write, only to its own attributes, only when its credentials are not temporarily overridden, only from the start of the file, and only up to a single page of data.
The writer identity and credential state are checked under read-side protection, and the actual security layer update runs while holding the caller credential guard mutex in interruptible mode.

Each supported security module gets a generated attribute subdirectory reusing the shared scan and enumerate helpers with its own entry table, plus getattr and no-chmod setattr handling. The top attribute directory lists the common attribute names and conditionally includes one subdirectory per compiled-in module.
The current, exec and creation attributes use mode 0666, the previous attribute uses 0444, and module subdirectories use 0555.

A per-process core dump filter is exposed as a small numeric file. Reading shows the current filter word extracted from the memory descriptor flags, and writing a number installs a new filter bit by bit.

The displayed value is the masked and shifted filter field rendered as fixed-width hexadecimal on one line. On write each bit of the supplied value sets or clears the corresponding filter flag in the target memory descriptor.
Operations that resolve a task, memory descriptor or user namespace from a file fail cleanly when the target has exited or is unavailable, returning a stale-handle style error without further action.
Per-thread and per-process-group I/O statistics are served from one shared routine with a flag selecting single-thread versus whole-group aggregation.

Statistics collection takes the target signal structure executable-update lock in killable read mode and verifies debugging access rights before touching counters. Group aggregation additionally runs under read-side protection with the statistics sequence lock held while summing the shared and per-thread counters.

The report always contains the same seven counters in fixed order covering characters moved, system call counts, storage byte counts and cancelled write bytes, each on its own labeled line as an unsigned decimal.
The first four I/O report lines are labeled rchar, wchar, syscr and syscw.
The remaining I/O report lines are labeled read_bytes, write_bytes and cancelled_write_bytes.

Identity map files capture a reference on the target user namespace at open, publish it through the sequential file private area for the duration of the open file, and drop the reference when the file is released.
User, group and project identity maps share read, seek and release handling while each binds its own open routine selecting the matching formatter and its own write routine.

A setgroups control file follows the same namespace capture pattern, but opening it for write additionally requires administrative privilege inside that namespace. Its release drops the namespace reference after the single-shot sequential state is torn down.
A shared release helper for single-shot sequential files tears down the sequential state and then frees the operation descriptor that was allocated for the one-shot display callback.

Several per-process attributes are rendered as one-line numeric reports: scheduling personality as fixed-width hexadecimal under trace protection, live-patch state as a plain integer with no locking, and kernel stack use as two labeled decimal lines for the previous and current depths derived from the thread stack markers.
Reading the scheduling personality serializes against concurrent tracing activity through the task trace lock.
Kernel same-page merging exposes a single counter file plus a multi-line statistics file, both resolving the target memory descriptor and reporting nothing when it is absent.
The statistics file reports rmap items, zero pages, merging pages and process profit as numbers, and shows the merge-any and mergeable states as yes or no words.
The mergeable probe in the same-page merging statistics runs under the target memory map read lock acquired in killable mode, released before the descriptor reference is dropped.
Opening a security attribute file records the opener address space so that later writes can verify the writer is the original opener.
Enumeration offers the dot entries first, then resumes the table at the stored position, ending cleanly once the position passes the last entry.

The per-process-group directory catalog defines subdirectories for lightweight tasks, open descriptors, descriptor details, mapped files, namespaces and networking, each pairing inode and file operation sets with restrictive or world-readable modes.

The same catalog registers regular and one-shot files covering environment, auxiliary vector, status summaries, scheduling controls, command line, memory maps, executable links, mount tables, resource usage and security attributes, with many entries present only under specific build options.
Selected catalog modes are 0555 for the task subdirectory, owner-only 0500 for descriptor and map file subdirectories, and world readable-writable 0666 for the timer slack file.

The group directory reuses the shared table scan and enumeration helpers over its catalog for lookup and listing, serves listings through the generic directory read path, and applies getattr, no-chmod setattr and process permission checks on its inodes.
A cross-file helper converts an open group directory file into its process identifier, rejecting files whose operations do not match the group directory set.
Numeric writes that fail to parse leave the target state untouched and propagate the parse failure to the caller.
